ground_truth_root_cause: A network partition between the three Kubernetes control-plane nodes at 14:06:10Z disrupted etcd cluster quorum, triggering a leader election (etcd term 47). During the roughly 2-minute election window, the kube-apiserver on all master nodes lost connectivity to etcd, causing it to reject all write operations including pod scheduling bindings. The existing cart-service pod (cart-7d9f8b-xkp2q) received a SIGTERM during the disruption and was evicted; replacement pods (cart-7d9f8b-nt3wp, cart-7d9f8b-rv9xc) were stuck in Pending state because the kube-scheduler could not commit scheduling decisions to etcd. This left cart-service with 0/3 replicas for approximately 4 minutes (14:06:19Z to 14:08:30Z) until etcd-2 was elected leader and normal scheduling resumed. This is entirely unrelated to any application-level deploy.
ground_truth_remediation: 1. Immediately verify etcd cluster health with etcdctl endpoint health --cluster and confirm all three etcd members have rejoined quorum under the new leader (etcd-2, term=47). 2. Investigate the network partition by reviewing CNI and switch logs between control-plane nodes around 14:06:00Z to identify the root cause such as a NIC flap, misconfigured network policy, or cloud provider network event. 3. Confirm cart-service is fully recovered with at least 2 of 3 replicas Running and passing health checks. 4. Short-term: increase etcd heartbeat and election timeouts to reduce sensitivity to transient network blips. 5. Long-term: add dedicated monitoring for etcd leader elections and control-plane network latency, and configure a PagerDuty alert for etcd quorum loss separate from application-level alerts.
red_herring: The checkout-service deploy (SHA d4f6b8a0c2e4d6b8f0a2c4d6e8b0a2c4d6e8b0a2, deployed at 11:55Z) upgraded the HTTP client library from v2.1 to v2.2, touching 14 files including cart_handler.go, transport.go, and retry.go which are components directly involved in checkout-to-cart communication. This change landed roughly 2 hours before the incident and is superficially suspicious because cart-service was the affected service and checkout-service is its primary downstream caller. An investigator might hypothesize that the new HTTP client introduced connection-pool exhaustion or a retry storm that overwhelmed cart-service. However, the logs provide clear exculpatory evidence: (1) at 14:03:00 to 14:03:01Z checkout-service logged successful initialization of the v2.2 HTTP client and confirmed cart-service was reachable, meaning the library worked correctly for over an hour before the incident with no errors; (2) cart-service itself continued serving requests normally until 14:06:19Z with sub-15ms latency and zero HTTP errors; (3) the failure mode was instantaneous 503s on all cart endpoints simultaneously rather than a gradual connection-pool degradation that a library change would cause; (4) logs at 14:06:10 through 14:06:24Z explicitly show etcd leader election messages, kube-apiserver etcd connectivity loss with context deadline exceeded and connection refused errors, and kube-scheduler failures to bind pods, none of which can be caused by an application-layer HTTP client change; and (5) recovery occurred at 14:08:10Z precisely when etcd elected a new leader, not when any deploy was rolled back.
